chunks: Ali ibn Ibrahim, from his father, from Ibn Abi Umayr, from Abd al-Rahman ibn al-Hajjaj, who said:

I sought permission for one of our companions to enter upon Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him), and he asked him about al-nabidh, so he said: 'It is permissible.' He said: 'May Allah keep you well, I only asked you about the nabidh in which the residue is placed and it boils until it intoxicates.'
Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) said: 'The Messenger of Allah (peace be upon him and his family) said: Every intoxicant is forbidden.'
The man said: 'May Allah keep you well, for those with us in Iraq say that the Messenger of Allah (peace be upon him and his family) only meant by that the cup that intoxicates.'
Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) said: 'Whatever a lot of it intoxicates, a little of it is forbidden.'
The man said to him: 'What if we dilute it with water?'
Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) said: 'No, and it is not for the water to make permissible that which is forbidden. Fear Allah, Mighty and Majestic, and do not drink it.'

key_terms.النَّبِيذ: Nabidh (fermented drink of water and fruit/dates)
key_terms.كَثِيرُهُ فَقَلِيلُهُ: A lot of it and a little of it

ai.seo_question: What is the ruling on nabidh if it intoxicates?
ai.summary: This hadith from al-Kafi clarifies the status of al-nabidh by establishing the principle of 'kathiruhu wa qaliluhu haram' (its abundant and scanty amounts are both forbidden) once intoxication occurs, refuting the Iraqi school's view that only the concentrated cup is prohibited. Imam al-Sadiq (AS) further emphasizes that dilution with water does not render the intoxicant permissible, underscoring the intrinsic nature of the prohibition. This ruling is foundational in Shia jurisprudence for determining the threshold of intoxication in fermented beverages.
